chunks: Multiphase and transient response. The question: How do they impact transient response?
When the load suddenly asks for more current, the inductor current cannot jump. It can only rise at a fixed rate.
In the meantime, the output capacitor covers the gap, and the output voltage dips. A multiphase buck raises the current faster, because several phases push at once.
It also allows a faster control loop. Both make the dip smaller.
Imagine a crowd suddenly rushing to a water fountain. The reservoir (the capacitor) gives out water at once while the pumps speed up.
One slow pump takes a long time to catch up, so the reservoir falls a lot. Four pumps working together catch up in a quarter of the time.
The analogy fits the slew-rate benefit, but it misses one thing: the capacitor's own small internal resistance (ESR) causes an instant dip that no converter speed can fix.
Small-signal droop for a 30 amps step with 1 mF, damping 0. 7.
The single-phase loop has a 50 kilohertz crossover (500 kilohertz over 10), while four phases allow 200 kilohertz (2 megahertz effective over 10).
The peak droop is about 44 millivolts versus 11 millivolts, and recovery is four times faster.
Load step: a sudden jump in the load current. Slew rate: how fast the inductor current can rise, (V in-V out) over L ("What sets the inductor current slope").
Effective inductance: with N phases pushing together, it is like one inductor of L over N ("What a multiphase buck is").
Droop: how far the output dips during a load step ("What happens in a load transient"). Loop crossover: how fast the control loop can respond.
A 12 volts to 1 volts converter has a 1 microhenries inductor per phase, so the current rises at 11 over 1 micro equals 11 amps/µs. A 30 amps step takes 30 over 11 about 2.
7 microseconds to catch up, with one phase. Four phases push together at 44 amps/µs, so the same step takes 30 over 44 about 0. 68 microseconds.
The capacitor covers a gap four times shorter. That is the whole idea.
"A multiphase buck responds faster for two reasons.
When the load steps, all phases ramp together, so the effective inductance is L over N and the total current slews N times faster, so the capacitor has to cover a much shorter gap.
And the effective sampling frequency is N times f sw, so the control loop can have a higher bandwidth.
For a 12 volts to 1 volts rail with a 30 amp step, four phases cut the ideal droop by about four times, so I can use roughly a quarter of the capacitance.
ESR and ESL still add their own instant step."
